zh.title: 第 1 部分｜M01：用白話文理解倫理駭客、CIA 與安全控制

sections.heading: 閱讀範圍：這次整理的九筆題號

body.text: 這份供稿原先提到「27 題」，本次第 1 部分實際提供九筆題號、參考答案與觀念解說，全部屬於 M01（倫理駭客入門），尚未包含 M20 密碼學；也沒有附上九題原題全文與所有選項。以下保留供稿的答案對照，作為知識複習線索，原題答案仍待取得完整題文後核對。
這九筆題號對應三個核心觀念：先理解觀念，再用理由回答不同問法，避免只背九組英文敘述。

items: 倫理駭客與授權：為什麼有人入侵系統是犯罪，有人卻是在合法執行滲透測試？
CIA 資訊安全三要素：資訊被偷看、被竄改、無法使用，分別代表什麼？
安全控制與縱深防禦：保全、門禁、防火牆、防毒軟體與加密，各自負責什麼？

sections.heading: 一、先看答案與題目對應關係

rows: 與 EC-Q001 相同的授權觀念
合法受聘的滲透測試人員
經授權的安全測試專業人員

body.text: 供稿依其題目敘述列出這些最佳答案。其中 P3-Q124 的 written permission 是正確的考試與實務方向，但完整的合法性還涉及授權者權限、測試範圍與適用法律。此處保留該判讀界線，不把未附題文的字母答案當成已獨立驗證的結果。

sections.heading: 二、為什麼有人駭入系統是犯罪，有人卻是白帽駭客？

body.text: 想像你經營一家銀行，想知道銀行的金庫夠不夠安全。你找來一位專業開鎖師傅，告訴他：「我想請你測試金庫的鎖，看小偷能不能打開。」
師傅用工具成功打開金庫，這是不是犯罪？不能只看他有沒有打開金庫，還要看他是否得到有效授權，以及是否遵守授權範圍。這就是倫理駭客（Ethical Hacking）的核心。
1. White Hat、Black Hat 與 Grey Hat 有什麼不同？

rows: 公司聘請滲透測試人員
未經授權，基於惡意目的入侵
可能沒有惡意，但缺乏授權
未經同意測試別人網站，再通知站長
依賴現成工具、技術理解通常有限
不懂原理就直接執行攻擊工具

body.text: Grey Hat 不代表合法；Script Kiddie 描述的是技術能力或行為方式，不是法律身分。而 Blue Hat 並沒有在所有教材中完全一致的定義，不適合當成通用的法律或職業分類。
2. 有授權就能做任何測試嗎？
不行。假設公司授權你測試時，同時訂下以下條件：

items: 只能在星期六上午 10 點至下午 2 點執行。
不可以進行阻斷服務（DoS）測試。

body.text: 你卻發現旁邊的 192.0.2.11 也有漏洞，便順便進去測試。即使你是公司聘請的白帽駭客，這項額外測試仍可能超出授權範圍。
這就是為什麼需要 Rules of Engagement（ROE，交戰規則）：在測試開始前，先說清楚誰能授權、測哪些目標、何時執行、哪些方法禁止，以及如何通報。

body.name: workflow
body.caption: 滲透測試的基本流程
body.description: 向下箭頭表示作業順序：先確認有效授權與範圍，再測試並追蹤改善；不表示取得授權後可以任意測試。

items.title: 定義 Scope 與 ROE
items.body: 測什麼？何時測？哪些方法禁止？

items.title: 在授權範圍內測試
items.body: 識別漏洞，控制影響，保留必要證據

items.title: 報告、修補、複測
items.body: 證明風險，追蹤改善效果

body.text: NIST 將 ROE 定義為資訊安全測試的詳細規則與限制，並要求在測試開始前建立。美國政府 ESC 的滲透測試服務也描述：雙方先簽署 ROE，約定目標、範圍、限制與通報，且只在約定時間對預定系統測試。[NIST ROE 定義](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/rules_of_engagement)；[ESC 滲透測試實務](https://www.esc.gov/Services/Cybersecurity/PenetrationTesting)。
EC-Q001、EC-Q054、EC-Q166、EC-Q476 都在考「獲得授權的安全測試者」這個概念，只是換了不同問法。
EC-Q189 強調最核心的區別是 permission（授權），而不是使用不同工具。白帽與黑帽甚至可能使用相同工具。
P3-Q124 考 written permission（書面授權）。實務上應在執行前取得可驗證的正式授權文件，而不是只依賴口頭同意。書面形式並非所有司法管轄區一律適用的單一合法標準。
EC-Q331 考倫理駭客的目標：找出漏洞並協助組織降低風險，而不是破壞或偷竊。測試人員通常負責發現、驗證與提出修補建議，不一定親自修改系統。

sections.heading: 三、CIA 三要素：資訊安全究竟在保護什麼？

body.text: 對應題目：P1-Q003。資訊安全不只是「不要讓駭客進來」。想像你經營一家醫院，電腦裡存放所有病人的病歷：保護目標包括保密性、完整性與可用性。

body.name: cia
body.caption: CIA：資訊安全三要素
body.description: 這三項是資訊安全最基本的保護目標，也是 NIST 所採用的核心概念。三欄是平行目標，不是先後流程。

items.title: C · Confidentiality
items.body:
保密性
不該看的人不能看

items.title: I · Integrity
items.body:
完整性
資料不能被擅自改壞

items.title: A · Availability
items.body:
可用性
需要時可以正常使用

body.text: CIA 的定義可回查 [NIST FIPS 199](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/199/final)；供稿所提的 [NIST SP 1800-26](https://www.nccoe.nist.gov/publication/1800-26/)則以破壞性事件的偵測與回應說明資料完整性問題。
1. Confidentiality：保密性
醫師把病歷寄給另一家醫院，卻使用沒有加密的通訊方式。結果，其他人只要攔截流量，就可能看見病人的姓名、病史與診斷結果。這是保密性出了問題。
題目中的關鍵字是 clear text（明文）、intercepting traffic（攔截流量）、unauthorized individuals view（未授權者查看）。因此供稿將 P1-Q003 對應為 B. Confidentiality。
常見的保護方式包括傳輸加密（例如適當設定的 TLS）、資料加密與權限控管。注意，傳輸加密與端對端加密並不完全相同。
2. Integrity：完整性
假設病人的血型原本是 A 型，有人擅自把資料改成 B 型。即使沒有其他人偷看病歷，資料也已經不可信。這是完整性問題。
常見保護措施包括雜湊驗證（Hash）、數位簽章（Digital Signature）、存取權限與資料變更稽核。比對雜湊時，預期雜湊值本身也需要可信來源；攻擊者若能同時替換資料與雜湊，單靠兩者一致不足以證明完整性。
3. Availability：可用性
假設醫院的掛號系統遭受阻斷服務攻擊，所有醫師與病人都無法登入。資料可能沒有外洩，也沒有被修改，但系統不能正常提供服務。這是可用性問題。
常見措施包括備援、流量防護、故障轉移與災難復原。
4. 那 Non-Repudiation 是什麼？
這是 P1-Q003 的另一個選項。Non-Repudiation（不可否認性）是指：能提供適當證據，使某個人或系統難以合理否認自己曾經執行特定行為。
例如某人簽署電子合約，之後卻聲稱：「這份合約不是我簽的。」若系統具有可信的數位簽章、身分驗證與紀錄機制，就能提高行為的可歸責性。
它與 CIA 有關，但在這個「資料遭偷看」的情境中，保密性是最直接的判斷。[NIST 不可否認性定義](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/non_repudiation)。

sections.heading: 四、Security Controls：為什麼保全也是資安的一部分？

body.text: 對應題目：P3-Q113。想像你有一家存放重要客戶資料的公司。你的伺服器防火牆設定得非常完善，也安裝了防毒軟體，但機房大門沒有上鎖。有人直接進入機房，偷走儲存裝置。
這時候你會發現：資訊安全不只是電腦軟體的問題。安全控制可以依實施方式分成幾個常見類型。

rows: 制定人員必須遵守的規範
安全政策、授權程序、教育訓練

body.text: 供稿將 P3-Q113 對應為 C. Security Guard。Security Guard（保全人員）是典型的實體安全控制。NIST SP 800-53 的 PE-3 也明確把保全人員列為控制設施出入的方式之一。[NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5，PE-3](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-53r5.pdf)。
縱深防禦（Defense in Depth）的想法，就是不要只依賴一道防線。例如下面五層可以相互補強；這是教學上的分層例子，實際系統的控制可能重疊運作。

items: 第一層：保全與門禁，阻止未授權人員進入機房。
第二層：帳號權限與多因素驗證，限制系統存取。
第三層：防火牆、端點防護，降低網路與主機攻擊風險。
第四層：加密與資料權限，降低敏感資料外洩的影響。
第五層：監控、事件應變與復原，處理已經發生的安全事件。

body.text: 不同控制措施可以相互補強，但不能保證完全不會遭到攻擊。

sections.heading: 五、這九題該如何複習才有效？

body.text: 不建議把九題當成九個獨立知識點反覆背誦。其中七筆題號都圍繞倫理駭客、有效授權及降低風險；另外兩筆分別連到保密性與實體安全控制。供稿這裡原寫「六題」，依上表九筆題號校對後更正為七筆。
可以把這份內容整理成三張主動回憶卡（Active Recall）：先自己說出答案，再展開參考答案，檢查是否包含適用條件與理由。第一張問題及對應題號依原圖保留，後兩張與三張答案依本文內容補成。

body.caption: 主動回憶卡（Active Recall）
body.description: 先在心裡作答，再翻開答案。卡片顯示與翻面只協助複習，不代表已理解或通過考試。

cards.question: 什麼條件讓滲透測試成為合乎規範的白帽行為？
answer: 先取得具有權限者的有效授權，明確約定測試目標、時段、方法限制與通報方式；在 Scope 與 ROE 內執行。
目標是識別、驗證漏洞並協助降低風險，留下報告與修補建議，再依約定複測。發現範圍外目標時，先停止該目標的主動測試，請求擴充授權。

cards.question: 病歷被偷看、血型被改壞、掛號系統無法使用，各影響 CIA 的哪一項？
answer: 未授權者偷看病歷：保密性（Confidentiality）。血型從 A 型被擅改為 B 型：完整性（Integrity）。掛號系統因阻斷服務無法使用：可用性（Availability）。
不可否認性關注行為證據與可歸責性，不是資料遭偷看最直接對應的目標。

cards.question: 為什麼有防火牆與加密，仍然需要保全和門禁？
answer: 保全與門禁保護實際場所和設備，屬於實體安全控制；防火牆與加密屬於技術控制；政策、授權程序與訓練屬於管理控制。
縱深防禦讓多種控制相互補強，涵蓋機房、人員、系統、資料及事件應變；任何單一控制都不能保證完全阻止攻擊。

body.text: 閱讀後，建議隔天、約三天後及一週後嘗試回憶；這些只是初始複習間隔，應依實際答題表現調整，不是固定適用所有人的遺忘曲線。

sections.heading: 六、理解檢核：三個實際情境

body.text: 這次不考你記不記得選項，而是檢查是否真的理解概念。選完三題後可在本頁取得解析；答案不儲存、不傳送，也不作正式考試或實作驗收紀錄。無 JavaScript 時，仍可逐題展開參考解析。

items.prompt: 公司書面授權你測試 A 系統。測試時發現 B 系統可能也有漏洞，但 B 不在授權範圍內。你應如何處理？
options: A. 只要目的是協助公司，就可以測試 B
B. 先停止對 B 的主動測試，請求擴充授權範圍
C. 只要使用免費工具，就不算違反授權
rationales: 善意目的不能取代對 B 系統的有效授權。
B 不在現有範圍內，應先停止對 B 的主動測試，取得有效的擴充授權後再執行。
工具是否免費與測試是否獲授權是不同問題。

items.prompt: 銀行的客戶資料沒有被偷看，但攻擊者修改了客戶的帳戶餘額。主要違反 CIA 的哪一項？
rationales: 保密性關注未授權的揭露；情境指出資料沒有被偷看。
帳戶餘額遭未授權修改，直接破壞資料完整性。
可用性關注需要時能否使用，情境未描述服務中斷。

items.prompt: 某公司部署了加密與防火牆，但任何人都能直接進入伺服器機房。最直接缺少哪一類安全控制？
rationales: 缺少對機房場所的出入限制，最直接需要實體安全控制。
加密可保護資料，不能直接阻止人員進入機房。
網路控制保護網路存取，不能取代保全與門禁。

body.text: 這份 M01 練習最值得牢記的核心是：授權決定你能不能測試，CIA 決定你要保護什麼，安全控制決定你用什麼方式保護。理解這三者的關係，就能延伸判斷其他不同情境的 CEH 題目。

en.title: Part 1 | M01: ethical hacking, CIA and security controls in plain language

sections.heading: Reading scope: the nine question references in this part

body.text: The supplied notes refer to “27 questions.” This first part actually provides nine question references, proposed answers and concept explanations, all in M01 (Introduction to Ethical Hacking). It does not yet include M20 cryptography, the full wording of the nine questions or all their options. The supplied answer mapping is retained as a study reference; checking the original answers requires the complete question texts.
These nine references connect to three core ideas. Understand the ideas and use reasoning to handle different phrasings, rather than memorizing nine English statements.

items: Ethical hacking and authorization: why can accessing a system be a crime in one case and an authorized penetration test in another?
The CIA triad: what is affected when information is viewed without permission, altered without permission or unavailable?
Security controls and defense in depth: what do guards, access controls, firewalls, antivirus software and encryption each protect?

sections.heading: 1. Map the supplied answers to concepts

rows: The same authorization concept as EC-Q001
A penetration tester engaged with valid authorization
Identify vulnerabilities and help get them remediated

body.text: The source presents these as the best answers for its question descriptions. Written permission in P3-Q124 is the appropriate exam-study and practice direction, while legality also depends on the authority of the person granting permission, the test scope and applicable law. That boundary is retained: a letter answer without the original question is not an independently verified result.

sections.heading: 2. Why can similar actions involve a criminal intruder or an authorized white hat?

body.text: Imagine that you run a bank and want to know whether its vault is secure. You hire a professional locksmith and say, “I want you to test the vault lock to see whether a thief could open it.”

The locksmith opens the vault with tools. Is that a crime? Opening the vault alone does not answer the question. You must also consider valid authorization and whether the locksmith stayed within its scope. This is central to ethical hacking.
1. How do white hats, black hats and grey hats differ?

rows: An organization hires a penetration tester
Intrudes without authorization for malicious purposes
Data theft, extortion or system damage
May lack malicious intent but lacks authorization
Tests a website without consent, then informs its operator
Relies on ready-made tools with typically limited technical understanding
Runs attack tools without understanding their mechanisms

body.text: Grey hat does not mean lawful. Script kiddie describes technical capability or behavior, not a legal status. Blue hat is not defined consistently across all teaching materials, so it should not be treated as a universal legal or occupational category.
2. Does authorization permit every kind of test?
No. Suppose a company authorizes a test with these conditions:

items: Test the server at 192.0.2.10.
Test only on Saturday from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.
Do not perform denial-of-service (DoS) tests.

body.text: You discover that the adjacent server, 192.0.2.11, also appears vulnerable and decide to test it too. Even as a hired white-hat tester, that additional activity may exceed the authorized scope.
This is why rules of engagement (ROE) are needed: establish who can authorize the work, the targets, the testing period, prohibited methods and notification procedures before the test begins.

body.name: workflow
body.caption: The basic penetration-testing workflow
body.description: Downward arrows indicate work order: establish valid authorization and scope, then test and follow up remediation. Authorization does not permit unrestricted testing.

items.title: Obtain valid authorization
items.body: Who has authority to approve the test?

items.title: Define scope and ROE
items.body: What, when and which methods are prohibited?

items.title: Test within the authorized scope
items.body: Identify vulnerabilities, control impact and retain necessary evidence

body.text: NIST defines ROE as detailed guidelines and constraints for information-security testing, established before testing begins. The U.S. government ESC penetration-testing service describes a signed ROE covering targets, scope, constraints and notifications, with testing restricted to agreed times and predetermined systems. [NIST ROE definition](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/rules_of_engagement); [ESC penetration-testing practice](https://www.esc.gov/Services/Cybersecurity/PenetrationTesting).
EC-Q001, EC-Q054, EC-Q166 and EC-Q476 all concern an authorized security tester, expressed through different wording.
EC-Q189 emphasizes permission as the central distinction, rather than different tools. White hats and black hats may even use the same tools.

P3-Q124 concerns written permission. In practice, obtain verifiable formal authorization before acting rather than relying only on verbal consent. Written form is not a single universal legal standard across every jurisdiction.

EC-Q331 concerns the purpose of ethical hacking: identify vulnerabilities and help the organization reduce risk, rather than cause damage or steal. Testers typically discover and validate findings and recommend remediation; they do not necessarily modify the systems themselves.

sections.heading: 3. The CIA triad: what does information security protect?

body.text: Related reference: P1-Q003. Information security involves more than keeping intruders out. Imagine a hospital whose computers store patient records: the protection goals include confidentiality, integrity and availability.

body.name: cia
body.caption: CIA: three information-security objectives
body.description: These are fundamental information-security objectives used by NIST. The three columns are parallel objectives, not sequential steps.

items.title: A · Availability
items.body:
Availability
Provide normal use when needed

body.text: For CIA definitions, see [NIST FIPS 199](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/199/final). The source also points to [NIST SP 1800-26](https://www.nccoe.nist.gov/publication/1800-26/), which discusses data integrity through detecting and responding to destructive events.
1. Confidentiality

A doctor sends patient records to another hospital using an unencrypted communication channel. Someone intercepting the traffic may see patient names, medical histories and diagnoses. This is a confidentiality problem.
The key phrases are clear text, intercepting traffic and unauthorized individuals view. The source therefore maps P1-Q003 to B. Confidentiality.
Common protections include encryption in transit, such as properly configured TLS, encryption of stored data and access controls. Encryption in transit and end-to-end encryption are not identical.
2. Integrity

Suppose a patient has blood type A, but someone changes the record to type B without authorization. Even if no one else reads the record, its data is no longer trustworthy. This is an integrity problem.

Common protections include hash verification, digital signatures, access permissions and audits of data changes. The expected hash must itself come from a trusted source: if an attacker can replace both the data and the hash, matching them alone does not establish integrity.
3. Availability

Suppose a denial-of-service attack hits the hospital registration system and doctors and patients cannot sign in. The data may remain undisclosed and unchanged, but the service cannot operate normally. This is an availability problem.
Common measures include redundancy, traffic protection, failover and disaster recovery.
4. What is non-repudiation?
This is another option mentioned for P1-Q003. Non-repudiation means providing suitable evidence that makes it difficult for a person or system to reasonably deny performing a particular action.

For example, a person signs an electronic contract but later says, “I did not sign this contract.” Trustworthy digital signatures, authentication and records can strengthen the evidence connecting the action to its actor.

Non-repudiation relates to CIA, but confidentiality is the direct concern in this unauthorized-viewing scenario. [NIST definition of non-repudiation](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/non_repudiation).

sections.heading: 4. Security controls: why are guards part of information security?

body.text: Related reference: P3-Q113. Imagine a company that stores important customer data. Its server firewall is carefully configured and antivirus software is installed, but the server-room door is unlocked. Someone walks in and steals a storage device.
The example shows why information security also involves the physical environment. Security controls are commonly grouped by how they are implemented.

rows: Guards, physical access controls and fences
Use technical mechanisms to protect systems
Define rules and procedures for people
Security policies, authorization procedures and training

body.text: The source maps P3-Q113 to C. Security Guard. A guard is a typical physical security control. PE-3 in NIST SP 800-53 explicitly includes guards among the ways to control entry and exit at a facility. [NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, PE-3](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-53r5.pdf).
Defense in depth means using several complementary protections. The following five layers illustrate the idea; in a real system, controls may overlap rather than operate as isolated stages.

items: Layer 1: guards and physical access controls prevent unauthorized entry into the server room.
Layer 2: account permissions and multifactor authentication restrict system access.
Layer 3: firewalls and endpoint protection reduce network and host attack risks.
Layer 4: encryption and data permissions reduce the impact of sensitive-data exposure.
Layer 5: monitoring, incident response and recovery address security incidents that have occurred.

body.text: Different controls reinforce each other, while attacks remain possible.

sections.heading: 5. How can you review these nine references effectively?

body.text: Do not treat the nine references as nine unrelated facts to memorize. Seven concern ethical hacking, valid authorization and risk reduction; the other two concern confidentiality and physical security controls. The source originally says “six” here; counting the references in the table gives seven.

Organize the content into three active-recall cards. First explain the answer yourself, then reveal the reference answer and check its conditions and reasoning. The first prompt and its references follow the supplied image; the other two prompts and all three answers are completed from the article content.

body.caption: Active Recall
body.description: Answer in your mind before revealing the answer. Viewing or revealing a card supports review; it does not establish understanding or exam readiness.

cards.question: What conditions make a penetration test a properly authorized white-hat activity?
answer: Obtain valid authorization from someone with the authority to grant it. Agree on targets, testing times, method restrictions and notifications, then work within the scope and ROE.

Identify and validate vulnerabilities to help reduce risk, provide a report and remediation recommendations, and retest as agreed. For an out-of-scope target, stop active testing of that target and request expanded authorization.

cards.question: Which CIA objective is affected by exposed records, an altered blood type and an unavailable registration system?
answer: Unauthorized viewing of records affects confidentiality. Changing blood type A to B without authorization affects integrity. A registration system disabled by denial of service affects availability.
Non-repudiation concerns evidence of actions and accountability; it is not the direct objective affected by unauthorized viewing.

cards.question: Why are guards and door access controls still needed when firewalls and encryption are in place?
answer: Guards and door access controls protect physical spaces and equipment and are physical controls. Firewalls and encryption are technical controls. Policies, authorization procedures and training are administrative controls.
Defense in depth combines protections for facilities, people, systems, data and incident response. No single control guarantees that every attack is prevented.

body.text: After reading, try recalling the material the next day, about three days later and a week later. These are initial review intervals to adjust according to actual performance, not a forgetting curve that applies identically to everyone.

sections.heading: 6. Check your understanding with three practical scenarios

body.text: These scenarios test your reasoning about the concepts. Select an answer for each to receive explanations on this page. Answers are neither stored nor transmitted and do not become official exam or practical-assessment records. Without JavaScript, you can still open each reference explanation.

items.prompt: A company gives you written authorization to test system A. During testing you notice that system B may also be vulnerable, but B is outside the authorized scope. What should you do?
options: A. Test B as long as your intention is to help the company
B. Stop active testing of B and request expanded authorization
C. Using free tools means the test does not violate authorization
rationales: Good intentions do not replace valid authorization for system B.
B is outside the current scope. Stop active testing of B and obtain valid expanded authorization before proceeding.
Whether a tool is free is separate from whether the test is authorized.

items.prompt: No one views bank customer data without permission, but an attacker changes account balances. Which CIA objective is primarily violated?
rationales: Confidentiality concerns unauthorized disclosure; the scenario says there was no unauthorized viewing.
Unauthorized changes to account balances directly compromise data integrity.
Availability concerns using a service when needed; the scenario does not describe an outage.

items.prompt: A company uses encryption and firewalls, but anyone can enter its server room. Which type of security control is most directly missing?
rationales: Unrestricted access to the server room most directly calls for physical security controls.
Encryption protects data but does not directly stop people entering the room.
Network controls protect network access and cannot replace guards or door access controls.

body.text: The central relationship in this M01 practice is: authorization determines whether you may test; CIA identifies what you protect; security controls describe how you protect it. Use this relationship to reason through other CEH scenarios.
